date.note: Solemnly promulgated by Pope Paul VI on 18 November 1965, during the fourth and final period of the Second Vatican Council (1962-1965). The Latin title Dei Verbum ('Word of God') is taken from the document's opening words.

summary: Dei Verbum ('Word of God') is the Dogmatic Constitution on Divine Revelation of the Second Vatican Council (1962-1965), promulgated by Pope Paul VI on 18 November 1965. It presents revelation as God's self-communication, treats sacred Scripture and sacred Tradition as flowing 'from the same divine wellspring', describes the teaching office as serving and not standing above the word of God, teaches the inspiration and inerrancy of Scripture for the sake of salvation, and encourages the reading of Scripture.
description:
Dei Verbum ('Word of God') is the Second Vatican Council's Dogmatic Constitution on Divine Revelation, promulgated by Pope Paul VI on 18 November 1965. Its Latin title is drawn from its opening words.

The constitution presents divine revelation as God's self-communication rather than only as the disclosure of truths. At DV 2 it states that 'in His goodness and wisdom God chose to reveal Himself and to make known to us the hidden purpose of His will', and it describes God addressing men as friends and inviting them into fellowship with himself. On the transmission of revelation, DV 9 sets sacred Tradition and sacred Scripture in close relation, teaching that 'both of them, flowing from the same divine wellspring, in a certain way merge into a unity and tend toward the same end.' On the relationship of the church's teaching office to revelation, DV 10 states that 'this teaching office is not above the word of God, but serves it, teaching only what has been handed on, listening to it devoutly, guarding it scrupulously and explaining it faithfully in accord with a divine commission and with the help of the Holy Spirit.'

On the inspiration and truth of Scripture, DV 11 affirms that the books of Scripture have God as their author and were written under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, and it frames their inerrancy in relation to the purpose of salvation: 'the books of Scripture must be acknowledged as teaching solidly, faithfully and without error that truth which God wanted put into sacred writings for the sake of salvation.' In its closing chapter the constitution encourages access to and reading of the Scriptures: at DV 22 it states that 'easy access to Sacred Scripture should be provided for all the Christian faithful', and at DV 25 it urges the reading of Scripture, citing the maxim that 'ignorance of the Scriptures is ignorance of Christ.' As a dogmatic constitution of the Roman Catholic Church, Dei Verbum articulates that church's teaching on revelation, Scripture, and Tradition; other Christian traditions hold differing accounts of the relationship of Scripture and Tradition and of the teaching office, and this entry presents the teaching as the council's own rather than as settled for all Christians, attributing every doctrinal claim to the document.
editorial_notes: This entry describes Dei Verbum on the council's own terms and attributes every doctrinal claim to the document and the Second Vatican Council, adjudicating nothing (neutrality #1, #2, #4, #6). It is a Roman Catholic dogmatic constitution; the entry flags that its account of revelation, Scripture, Tradition, and the teaching office is the council's own and that other Christian traditions differ (notably on the relation of Scripture and Tradition), without ranking any position. The load-bearing phrases were read directly on the open official English text at vatican.va and are quoted verbatim: DV 2 'in His goodness and wisdom God chose to reveal Himself and to make known to us the hidden purpose of His will'; DV 9 'flowing from the same divine wellspring, in a certain way merge into a unity and tend toward the same end'; DV 10 'this teaching office is not above the word of God, but serves it, teaching only what has been handed on ...'; DV 11 'teaching solidly, faithfully and without error that truth which God wanted put into sacred writings for the sake of salvation'; DV 22 'easy access to Sacred Scripture should be provided for all the Christian faithful'; and DV 25 'ignorance of the Scriptures is ignorance of Christ'. Sources triangulate three lenses per neutrality #8-#9: (b) the primary text itself, the official English translation open at vatican.va, rated HIGH because the quoted phrases above were read line-by-line and confirmed on the page; (a) an academic historian of the council, John W. O'Malley, What Happened at Vatican II (Belknap/Harvard, 2008), medium, verified to exist and on-topic; and (c) a contemporary Catholic theologian, Ormond Rush, Still Interpreting Vatican II: Some Hermeneutical Principles (Paulist, 2004), medium, verified to exist and on-topic (Rush reads the council through the theological focus of Dei Verbum on revelation as God's self-communication). No encyclopedias, no Wikipedia, no tertiary sources. relations.note: Dei Verbum is one of the four constitutions of the Second Vatican Council, promulgated during its fourth period on 18 November 1965. The second-vatican-council event entity exists in the dataset.

Debated, amended, and solemnly promulgated by Pope Paul VI with the council fathers at the Second Vatican Council (1962-1965); recorded as produced by the council. The second-vatican-council event entity exists in the dataset.

A companion dogmatic constitution of the same council (promulgated 21 November 1964); Dei Verbum on divine revelation and Lumen Gentium on the Church are the council's two dogmatic constitutions. The lumen-gentium entry is authored alongside this one.

sources.citation: O'Malley, John W. What Happened at Vatican II. Cambridge, MA: The Belknap Press of Harvard University Press, 2008 (ISBN 9780674031692). A peer-reviewed academic historian's narrative history of the Second Vatican Council from its announcement (1959) to its close (1965), based on the official documentation, treating the drafting and adoption of Dei Verbum and the other constitutions; cited as the outside-scholarship lens. Verified to exist and be on-topic via the Harvard University Press catalog and journal reviews (Journal of Ecclesiastical History; Journal of Religion), not read line-by-line here.

Rush, Ormond. Still Interpreting Vatican II: Some Hermeneutical Principles. New York: Paulist Press, 2004 (ISBN 9780809142859). A contemporary Catholic theologian's study of the interpretation of the Second Vatican Council that gives a central place to Dei Verbum, reading revelation as God's self-communication and an encounter with God in Christ through the Holy Spirit; cited as the contemporary-Catholic-theologian lens. Verified to exist and be on-topic via the Paulist Press / Google Books records, not read line-by-line here.
